Corporate Thursday, January 28, 2021, 6:00 a.m.

# American Airlines Reports Fourth-Quarter and Full-Year 2020 Financial Results

Share this article

[![Image 2: Twitter](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/design/svg/tw.svg)](https://news.aa.com/#twitter)[![Image 3: Facebook](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/design/facebookIcon.svg)](https://news.aa.com/#facebook)[![Image 4: LinkedIn](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/design/linkedInIcon.svg)](https://news.aa.com/#linkedin)[![Image 5: eMail](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/design/emailIcon.svg)](https://news.aa.com/#email)

[Newsroom](https://news.aa.com/overview/default.aspx)>[News](https://news.aa.com/news/default.aspx)> Press Release Details 

![Image 6](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/doc_news/2021/01/1/social-American-Airlines-generic-20.jpg)

FORT WORTH, Texas — American Airlines Group Inc. (NASDAQ: AAL) today reported its fourth-quarter and full-year 2020 financial results, including: Fourth-quarter revenue of $4.0 billion, down 64% year over year on a 53% year-over-year reduction in total available seat miles (ASMs).

[![Image 7: 2Q 2020 Financial Results](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/doc_news/2021/01/1/4Q20-Financial-Results-Fact-Sheet.png)](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/doc_news/2021/01/1/4Q20-Financial-Results-Fact-Sheet.pdf)
[Click to download](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/doc_news/2021/01/1/4Q20-Financial-Results-Fact-Sheet.pdf)

FORT WORTH, Texas — American Airlines Group Inc. (NASDAQ: AAL) today reported its fourth-quarter and full-year 2020 financial results, including:

*   **Fourth-quarter revenue of $4.0 billion, down 64% year over year on a 53% year-over-year reduction in total available seat miles (ASMs).**
*   **Fourth-quarter net loss of $2.2 billion, or ($3.81) per share. Excluding net special items 1, fourth-quarter net loss was $2.2 billion, or ($3.86) per share.**
*   **Full-year net loss of $8.9 billion, or ($18.36) per share. Excluding net special items 2, full-year net loss was $9.5 billion, or ($19.66) per share.**
*   **Ended fourth quarter with approximately $14.3 billion of total available liquidity. Company expects to end the first quarter of 2021 with approximately $15.0 billion in total available liquidity.**
*   **Incorporated more than $1.3 billion of permanent non-volume, non-fuel efficiency cost-saving measures into 2021 operating plan.**

“Our fourth-quarter financial results close out the most challenging year in our company’s history,” said American Airlines Chairman and CEO Doug Parker. “However, we couldn’t be prouder of the American Airlines team and the great things they accomplished last year. Through collaboration, resourcefulness and hard work, our team did its part to keep the economy moving. The American team flew more customers than any other airline in 2020, and they did so safely and with the utmost care.

“As we look to the year ahead, 2021 will be a year of recovery. While we don’t know exactly when passenger demand will return, as vaccine distribution takes hold and travel restrictions are lifted, we will be ready. We are confident that the actions we have taken to improve our customer experience, enhance our network and increase our efficiency position us well for the future.”

American took a number of steps in 2020 to respond to the pandemic and strengthen its business, with an emphasis on supporting its team members, customers and communities; reducing costs; and improving its liquidity position.

## To support its team members, customers and communities, American:

*   [Enhanced](https://www.aa.com/i18n/travel-info/travel-with-confidence.jsp)​ its cleaning procedures at airports and onboard aircraft under the guidance of its Travel Health Advisory Panel, earning the STAR® Accreditation from the Global Biorisk Advisory Council for effective cleaning, disinfection and infectious disease prevention practices onboard its aircraft and in its lounges.
*   Introduced a preflight coronavirus (COVID-19) testing program to help reopen certain international travel markets. American now offers testing for many international destinations and has introduced at-home testing for customers traveling to all U.S. locations that require negative tests.
*   Began the rollout of mobile wellness wallet solution VeriFLY to make domestic and international travel simpler. Travelers can now easily understand COVID-19 testing and documentation requirements for their destination and streamline airport check-in through digital verification. Starting today, customers also will be able to use VeriFLY for travel from the United States to the U.K. and Canada.
*   Eliminated fees for:

    *   Ticket changes on all domestic and international itineraries when traveling from North and South America, with the exception of Basic Economy fares that are nonchangeable.
    *   Mileage redeposits for canceled award bookings.
    *   Domestic same-day standby.
    *   Booking reservations by phone.

*   Made it easier for top-tier customers to earn AAdvantage® elite status in 2020 and 2021, paused mileage expiration through June 30, 2021, and extended 2020 AAdvantage status into early 2022 for all members.
*   Launched the company’s first cargo-only flights since 1984 to transport critical goods, including the COVID-19 vaccine, and increased service to include 41 destinations for strategic cargo-only opportunities. American helped customers move nearly 800 million pounds of critical goods around the world in 2020, including 167 million pounds on the airline’s more than 5,200 cargo-only flights.
*   Announced its goal to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2050 and detailed the company’s strategy and pathway in its [ESG Report](https://www.aa.com/i18n/customer-service/about-us/environmental-social-governance.jsp).

## To reduce costs and conserve cash, American:

*   Removed more than $17 billion from its operating and capital budgets for 2020 primarily through reduced flying.
*   Incorporated more than $1.3 billion of permanent non-volume, non-fuel efficiency cost-saving measures into 2021 operating plan.
*   Retired five aircraft types (Embraer 190, Boeing 757, Boeing 767, Airbus A330 and Bombardier CRJ200), along with a number of older regional aircraft. The company also placed certain older Boeing 737-800 aircraft into temporary storage. These changes removed more than 150 aircraft from the fleet and brought forward significant cost savings and efficiencies associated with operating fewer aircraft types, giving American the youngest fleet among the U.S. network carriers.
*   Reached an agreement with Boeing to secure rights to defer deliveries of 18 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft and finalized a series of sale-leaseback transactions to finance its Airbus A321 aircraft deliveries in 2021. To date, five of the 18 737 MAX deferral rights have been exercised.
*   Reset its international capacity and network for 2021, including exiting 19 international routes from six hubs.
*   Reduced non-aircraft capital expense by $700 million in 2020 and another $300 million in 2021 through reductions in fleet modification work, the elimination of ground service equipment purchases, and pausing noncritical facility investments and IT projects.
*   Introduced programs to right-size its frontline and management teams. In total, more than 20,000 team members opted to participate in a voluntary early out or long-term partially paid leave during the year, and the company reduced its management and support staff team by approximately 30%.
*   Made the difficult decision to proceed with furloughs to reduce headcount absent an extension of the CARES Act Payroll Support Program (PSP). American’s furloughed team members have since had their pay and benefits reinstated with the passage of a bipartisan COVID-19 relief package that renewed the PSP from Dec. 1, 2020, through March 31, 2021.

## To improve its liquidity position, American:

*   Reduced its daily cash burn rate 3 from nearly $100 million in April 2020 to approximately $30 million in the fourth quarter. This improvement was driven by the company’s revenue and cost-reduction initiatives throughout the year.
*   Secured approximately $9 billion in financial assistance through two rounds of PSP legislation and executed an agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury through the CARES Act loan program that gives the company access to up to $7.5 billion of secured term loans, of which $550 million has been drawn.
*   Raised more than $13 billion during the year through various other equity and debt offerings.
*   Expects to end the first quarter with approximately $15.0 billion in total available liquidity.

## Network and partnerships

American reset its network in 2020 to play to the strengths of its hubs and take advantage of its younger and simplified fleet. The airline also established new and innovative partnerships with Alaska Airlines and JetBlue Airways that will create the best and largest network for customers on the West Coast and in the Northeast. These partnerships will allow for efficient growth, including the launch of new service in 2021 between Seattle and London, Shanghai and Bangalore, and between New York and Tel Aviv and Athens.

## Demand and capacity outlook

The company will continue to match its forward capacity with observed bookings trends. Compared to the first quarter of 2019, American expects its first-quarter system capacity to be down 45%, with total revenue expected to be down 60 to 65%.

## Conference call and webcast details

The company will conduct a live audio webcast of its financial results call at 7:30 a.m. CST today. The call will be available to the public on a listen-only basis at [aa.com/investorrelations](http://www.aa.com/investorrelations). An archive of the webcast will be available on the website through Feb. 28.

## Notes

1 See the accompanying notes in the Financial Tables section of this press release for further explanation, including a reconciliation of all GAAP to non-GAAP financial information.

The company recognized $36 million of nonoperating net special items during the fourth quarter of 2020. These net special items principally included mark-to-market net unrealized gains and losses associated with certain equity investments and treasury rate lock derivative instruments.

2 The 2020 12-month period mainline operating special items, net principally included $3.7 billion of PSP financial assistance, offset in part by $1.5 billion of fleet impairment charges, $1.4 billion of salary and medical costs primarily associated with certain team members who opted in to voluntary early retirement programs offered as a result of reductions to the company's operation due to COVID-19, and $228 million of one-time labor contract expenses resulting from the ratification of a new contract with the company's maintenance and fleet service team members, including signing bonuses and adjustments to vacation accruals resulting from pay rate increases.

The 2020 12-month period regional operating special items, net principally included $444 million of PSP financial assistance, offset in part by $117 million of fleet impairment charges and $18 million of salary and medical costs primarily associated with the voluntary early retirement programs as discussed above.

The company recognized $170 million of nonoperating net special items in 2020. These net special items principally included mark-to-market net unrealized gains and losses associated with certain equity investments and treasury rate lock derivative instruments as well as charges associated with debt refinancings and extinguishments.

# American Airlines Reports Fourth-Quarter and Full-Year 2020 Financial Results

[![Image 2: Twitter](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/design/svg/tw.svg)](https://news.aa.com/#twitter)[![Image 3: Facebook](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/design/facebookIcon.svg)](https://news.aa.com/#facebook)[![Image 4: LinkedIn](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/design/linkedInIcon.svg)](https://news.aa.com/#linkedin)[![Image 5: eMail](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/design/emailIcon.svg)](https://news.aa.com/#email)

![Image 6](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/doc_news/2021/01/1/social-American-Airlines-generic-20.jpg)

FORT WORTH, Texas — American Airlines Group Inc. (NASDAQ: AAL) today reported its fourth-quarter and full-year 2020 financial results, including: Fourth-quarter revenue of $4.0 billion, down 64% year over year on a 53% year-over-year reduction in total available seat miles (ASMs).

[![Image 7: 2Q 2020 Financial Results](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/doc_news/2021/01/1/4Q20-Financial-Results-Fact-Sheet.png)](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/doc_news/2021/01/1/4Q20-Financial-Results-Fact-Sheet.pdf)
[Click to download](https://s202.q4cdn.com/986123435/files/doc_news/2021/01/1/4Q20-Financial-Results-Fact-Sheet.pdf)

FORT WORTH, Texas — American Airlines Group Inc. (NASDAQ: AAL) today reported its fourth-quarter and full-year 2020 financial results, including:

*   **Fourth-quarter revenue of $4.0 billion, down 64% year over year on a 53% year-over-year reduction in total available seat miles (ASMs).**
*   **Fourth-quarter net loss of $2.2 billion, or ($3.81) per share. Excluding net special items 1, fourth-quarter net loss was $2.2 billion, or ($3.86) per share.**
*   **Full-year net loss of $8.9 billion, or ($18.36) per share. Excluding net special items 2, full-year net loss was $9.5 billion, or ($19.66) per share.**
*   **Ended fourth quarter with approximately $14.3 billion of total available liquidity. Company expects to end the first quarter of 2021 with approximately $15.0 billion in total available liquidity.**
*   **Incorporated more than $1.3 billion of permanent non-volume, non-fuel efficiency cost-saving measures into 2021 operating plan.**

“Our fourth-quarter financial results close out the most challenging year in our company’s history,” said American Airlines Chairman and CEO Doug Parker. “However, we couldn’t be prouder of the American Airlines team and the great things they accomplished last year. Through collaboration, resourcefulness and hard work, our team did its part to keep the economy moving. The American team flew more customers than any other airline in 2020, and they did so safely and with the utmost care.

“As we look to the year ahead, 2021 will be a year of recovery. While we don’t know exactly when passenger demand will return, as vaccine distribution takes hold and travel restrictions are lifted, we will be ready. We are confident that the actions we have taken to improve our customer experience, enhance our network and increase our efficiency position us well for the future.”

American took a number of steps in 2020 to respond to the pandemic and strengthen its business, with an emphasis on supporting its team members, customers and communities; reducing costs; and improving its liquidity position.

## To support its team members, customers and communities, American:

*   [Enhanced](https://www.aa.com/i18n/travel-info/travel-with-confidence.jsp)​ its cleaning procedures at airports and onboard aircraft under the guidance of its Travel Health Advisory Panel, earning the STAR® Accreditation from the Global Biorisk Advisory Council for effective cleaning, disinfection and infectious disease prevention practices onboard its aircraft and in its lounges.
*   Introduced a preflight coronavirus (COVID-19) testing program to help reopen certain international travel markets. American now offers testing for many international destinations and has introduced at-home testing for customers traveling to all U.S. locations that require negative tests.
*   Began the rollout of mobile wellness wallet solution VeriFLY to make domestic and international travel simpler. Travelers can now easily understand COVID-19 testing and documentation requirements for their destination and streamline airport check-in through digital verification. Starting today, customers also will be able to use VeriFLY for travel from the United States to the U.K. and Canada.
*   Eliminated fees for:

    *   Ticket changes on all domestic and international itineraries when traveling from North and South America, with the exception of Basic Economy fares that are nonchangeable.
    *   Mileage redeposits for canceled award bookings.
    *   Domestic same-day standby.
    *   Booking reservations by phone.

*   Made it easier for top-tier customers to earn AAdvantage® elite status in 2020 and 2021, paused mileage expiration through June 30, 2021, and extended 2020 AAdvantage status into early 2022 for all members.
*   Launched the company’s first cargo-only flights since 1984 to transport critical goods, including the COVID-19 vaccine, and increased service to include 41 destinations for strategic cargo-only opportunities. American helped customers move nearly 800 million pounds of critical goods around the world in 2020, including 167 million pounds on the airline’s more than 5,200 cargo-only flights.
*   Announced its goal to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2050 and detailed the company’s strategy and pathway in its [ESG Report](https://www.aa.com/i18n/customer-service/about-us/environmental-social-governance.jsp).

## To reduce costs and conserve cash, American:

*   Removed more than $17 billion from its operating and capital budgets for 2020 primarily through reduced flying.
*   Incorporated more than $1.3 billion of permanent non-volume, non-fuel efficiency cost-saving measures into 2021 operating plan.
*   Retired five aircraft types (Embraer 190, Boeing 757, Boeing 767, Airbus A330 and Bombardier CRJ200), along with a number of older regional aircraft. The company also placed certain older Boeing 737-800 aircraft into temporary storage. These changes removed more than 150 aircraft from the fleet and brought forward significant cost savings and efficiencies associated with operating fewer aircraft types, giving American the youngest fleet among the U.S. network carriers.
*   Reached an agreement with Boeing to secure rights to defer deliveries of 18 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft and finalized a series of sale-leaseback transactions to finance its Airbus A321 aircraft deliveries in 2021. To date, five of the 18 737 MAX deferral rights have been exercised.
*   Reset its international capacity and network for 2021, including exiting 19 international routes from six hubs.
*   Reduced non-aircraft capital expense by $700 million in 2020 and another $300 million in 2021 through reductions in fleet modification work, the elimination of ground service equipment purchases, and pausing noncritical facility investments and IT projects.
*   Introduced programs to right-size its frontline and management teams. In total, more than 20,000 team members opted to participate in a voluntary early out or long-term partially paid leave during the year, and the company reduced its management and support staff team by approximately 30%.
*   Made the difficult decision to proceed with furloughs to reduce headcount absent an extension of the CARES Act Payroll Support Program (PSP). American’s furloughed team members have since had their pay and benefits reinstated with the passage of a bipartisan COVID-19 relief package that renewed the PSP from Dec. 1, 2020, through March 31, 2021.

## To improve its liquidity position, American:

*   Reduced its daily cash burn rate 3 from nearly $100 million in April 2020 to approximately $30 million in the fourth quarter. This improvement was driven by the company’s revenue and cost-reduction initiatives throughout the year.
*   Secured approximately $9 billion in financial assistance through two rounds of PSP legislation and executed an agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury through the CARES Act loan program that gives the company access to up to $7.5 billion of secured term loans, of which $550 million has been drawn.
*   Raised more than $13 billion during the year through various other equity and debt offerings.
*   Expects to end the first quarter with approximately $15.0 billion in total available liquidity.

## Network and partnerships

American reset its network in 2020 to play to the strengths of its hubs and take advantage of its younger and simplified fleet. The airline also established new and innovative partnerships with Alaska Airlines and JetBlue Airways that will create the best and largest network for customers on the West Coast and in the Northeast. These partnerships will allow for efficient growth, including the launch of new service in 2021 between Seattle and London, Shanghai and Bangalore, and between New York and Tel Aviv and Athens.

## Demand and capacity outlook

The company will continue to match its forward capacity with observed bookings trends. Compared to the first quarter of 2019, American expects its first-quarter system capacity to be down 45%, with total revenue expected to be down 60 to 65%.

## Conference call and webcast details

The company will conduct a live audio webcast of its financial results call at 7:30 a.m. CST today. The call will be available to the public on a listen-only basis at [aa.com/investorrelations](http://www.aa.com/investorrelations). An archive of the webcast will be available on the website through Feb. 28.

## Notes

1 See the accompanying notes in the Financial Tables section of this press release for further explanation, including a reconciliation of all GAAP to non-GAAP financial information.

The company recognized $36 million of nonoperating net special items during the fourth quarter of 2020. These net special items principally included mark-to-market net unrealized gains and losses associated with certain equity investments and treasury rate lock derivative instruments.

2 The 2020 12-month period mainline operating special items, net principally included $3.7 billion of PSP financial assistance, offset in part by $1.5 billion of fleet impairment charges, $1.4 billion of salary and medical costs primarily associated with certain team members who opted in to voluntary early retirement programs offered as a result of reductions to the company's operation due to COVID-19, and $228 million of one-time labor contract expenses resulting from the ratification of a new contract with the company's maintenance and fleet service team members, including signing bonuses and adjustments to vacation accruals resulting from pay rate increases.

The 2020 12-month period regional operating special items, net principally included $444 million of PSP financial assistance, offset in part by $117 million of fleet impairment charges and $18 million of salary and medical costs primarily associated with the voluntary early retirement programs as discussed above.

The company recognized $170 million of nonoperating net special items in 2020. These net special items principally included mark-to-market net unrealized gains and losses associated with certain equity investments and treasury rate lock derivative instruments as well as charges associated with debt refinancings and extinguishments.

## Introduction

American Airlines Group is the third-largest U.S. airline by 2025 operating revenue, behind Delta and United, and operates one of the most extensive U.S. route networks (DOT BTS data), connecting high-yield corporate markets through hubs in Dallas-Fort Worth (approximately 925 of about 1,100 daily departures, roughly 84%, based on 2024 DFW operating data and BTS T-100), Charlotte, and Miami. With **$54.2 billion in then-record full-year 2024 operating revenue** (since surpassed by FY2025's $54.6 billion), American demonstrated profitability with approximately 3% year-over-year revenue growth per the 2024 10-K; about 224 million passengers boarded its flights in 2025 (FY2025 Form 10-K). However, American's financial story reflects **$30.48 billion in long-term debt at year-end 2024 (the company's largest reported debt line; AAL's company-defined total debt — which includes finance and operating lease obligations and pension obligations — was approximately $39B at year-end 2024, the highest among the Big 3 carriers)** — and **negative total equity of approximately ($4 billion)**, putting lease-adjusted debt/EBITDAR at 7.9x for FY2025 — $35.97 billion of debt, finance leases and operating lease liabilities against EBITDAR of $4.58 billion, which is DWU's own arithmetic on four lines AAG prints in its FY2025 Form 10-K, against lower ratios at Delta and United. No Form 10-K prints this ratio for any of the three carriers; the arithmetic is shown in the leverage section below.

American's financial position reflects advantages (84% DFW hub share) and structural risks (lease-adjusted debt/EBITDAR of 7.9x for FY2025 on DWU's arithmetic, against lower peer ratios): (1) the airline operates its largest hub by daily departures (DFW with approximately 925 daily departures, about 84% of ~1,100 total, BTS T-100 2024; among the most single-carrier-concentrated large hubs, though American's Charlotte hub carries an even higher share), which enables connections to 300+ destinations and influences local fares (BTS T-100 2024); (2) the AAdvantage loyalty program produces approximately **$6.1 billion in annual cash remuneration** from co-branded credit-card and loyalty-marketing agreements (up 17% in 2024 per the 10-K) — a cash-flow measure recognized within passenger and other revenue, not a separate additive revenue line; this stream tends to be less volatile than passenger revenue; yet (3) a 2023-2024 strategy shift to direct corporate accounts weighed on American's unit-revenue (Passenger Revenue per Available Seat Mile, PRASM) performance relative to peers during 2024, prompting the reversal announced in mid-2024 (AA earnings calls); by the fourth quarter of 2024 American's passenger unit revenue had returned to year-over-year growth (AA Q4/FY2024 release). This profile examines American's financial structure, operational challenges, strategic recovery, and credit dynamics.

## Company Overview

### History and Structural Legacy

American Airlines was founded in 1926. That predates Delta (1928) and United (1926 reorganization) among major U.S. carriers. The 2013 merger with US Airways created American Airlines Group (AAG). It became the world's largest airline by fleet size (approximately 1,000 mainline aircraft plus regional partners, 10-K 2024) and passengers carried, surpassing Delta and United. The merger unified two legacy carriers with overlapping networks. It also created post-merger integration challenges documented in American's 2014-2016 10-K filings around fleet utilization, crew bases, and integration costs. See [Airline Bankruptcy and Restructuring History](https://dwuconsulting.com/dwu-ai/airline-bankruptcy-restructuring-history) for context on post-merger integration outcomes.

Headquartered in Fort Worth, Texas, American operates under International Air Transport Association (IATA) code **AA** and International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) code **AAL**. The airline maintains significant operations at [Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport (DFW)](https://web.archive.org/web/https://www.dfwairport.com/about/), its largest hub, and at [Charlotte Douglas International (CLT)](https://www.cltairport.com/), its second-largest hub. American is a founding member of the **Oneworld Alliance**, providing global codeshare access to British Airways, Japan Airlines, Cathay Pacific, and others.

As of 2024, American employs approximately 133,300 team members system-wide across all functions (10-K 2024). It is a major employer in the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex, where it is headquartered.

### Strategic Market Position

American operates a domestic network spanning corporate markets including New York, Washington DC, Los Angeles, Miami, Boston, and Philadelphia. The airline reported a 2024 PRASM of 16.93¢/mile (10-K 2024). About 224 million passengers boarded American's flights in 2025 (FY2025 Form 10-K).

#### Airport Planning Considerations

American's debt structure and negative equity matter for airport tenant-risk monitoring, traffic-risk scenario planning, and air-service strategy at the airports it dominates. They do not directly drive Passenger Facility Charge (PFC) spending, however. PFC use is governed by statutory eligibility, FAA approval, project funding structure, and the no-double-charge rules, not by a carrier's balance sheet. Airports may consider carrier credit metrics and debt refinancing schedules in scenario planning for revenue patterns and service continuity (DOT BTS data).

Conversely, American's 84% departure share at DFW (BTS T-100, 2024) provides the carrier with network leverage and pricing power. From the airport's perspective, however, single-carrier concentration above 50% is a credit-rating consideration under S&P and Fitch airport methodologies. DFW's investment-grade rating rests on underlying revenue resilience, liquidity, its rate-setting methodology and AUA protections, strategic importance, and a substantial non-airline revenue base, even as American's departure share remains high. PFCs can offset eligible capital and debt service but are restricted, project-specific revenues. Debt-service-coverage covenants are bondholder protections and tests rather than diversification mechanisms in their own right. Free cash flow: $2.2B (2024 10-K).

## Hub Network and Competitive Positioning

### Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW) — American's Largest Hub by Daily Departures

Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) is American's flagship hub with approximately 84% of daily departures (about 925 of 1,100 daily departures based on DFW airport operating data + BTS T-100 2024; mainline departures inclusive of regional affiliates). American controls approximately 925 daily departures and serves more than 230 nonstop destinations from DFW. This roughly 84% departure share exceeds Delta's approximately 75% at Atlanta and United's share at Chicago ORD (BTS T-100 2024), providing American with:

**Network Leverage:** Domestic connectivity via 300+ destinations (BTS T-100 2024). A passenger from Austin, San Antonio, or anywhere in the Texas, Oklahoma, or Arkansas region can reach virtually any major U.S. market through DFW, often with a single connection.

**Pricing Power:** At DFW's 84% departure share, American's hub concentration supports network pricing power and can influence local fares in some markets (Dallas to New York, Dallas to Los Angeles). Route-level fare effects, however, depend on origin-and-destination (O&D) demand and competitive capacity rather than departure share alone.

**Operational Efficiency:** The scale of DFW operations — 925 daily American flights out of DFW's 1,100 total daily flights — justifies investment in premium ground infrastructure, crew scheduling, and customer service.

**Corporate Travel Concentration:** DFW serves the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex, a metro area of approximately 8.3 million people (U.S. Census Bureau). It is home to corporate headquarters including Texas Instruments (technology), AT&T (telecommunications), and American Airlines Group (aviation), along with numerous Fortune 500 companies. This corporate base generates premium-cabin and business-travel demand from major employers.

### Charlotte (CLT) — Second Hub and Growth Market

Charlotte Douglas International Airport is American's second-largest hub, where American holds a high share of daily departures and serves a broad domestic network (BTS T-100 2024). CLT anchors American's hub in Charlotte's banking and corporate market (the Research Triangle/Raleigh-Durham region is served by its own airport, RDU). The Charlotte metropolitan area has been among the faster-growing large U.S. metros (U.S. Census Bureau). American's hub status at CLT provides strong pricing influence.

### Miami (MIA) — Caribbean and Latin American Gateway

Miami serves as American's Latin American and Caribbean gateway, serving as a gateway to major Caribbean and Latin American markets (BTS T-100 2024). Miami-Dade County has a majority-Hispanic population (U.S. Census Bureau), supporting connectivity to Central and South America (BTS T-100 2024).

## Strategic Shifts and 2024 Adjustments

### Corporate Travel Strategy Shift

In 2023-2024, American management under CEO Robert Isom shifted to direct corporate accounts. That weighed on the airline's unit-revenue (PRASM) performance relative to peers during 2024 (AA 2024 earnings calls). The shift created several challenges.

**The challenges of the strategy:** Corporate travelers book through their companies' preferred travel management companies (TMCs like American Express Global Business Travel, BCD Travel, etc.), which receive commissions from airlines and can negotiate volume discounts. American's attempt to bypass TMCs and shift corporate bookings to direct channels led to reduced bookings via TMCs (AA Q4 2024 earnings).

**Competitive Disadvantage:** Delta and United maintained strong TMC partnerships and actively competed for corporate business, capturing market share from American. Corporate travel yields higher fares, more first/business class upgrades, and better liquidity profile — making this loss particularly damaging.

**Yield Compression:** American's PRASM lagged competitors particularly in mid-2024 (AA 2024 earnings calls).

### Management Acknowledgment and Strategic Reversal

On the Q4 2024 earnings call (January 23, 2025), CEO Robert Isom acknowledged that American's 2023-2024 corporate travel strategy had weighed on the airline's unit-revenue performance during 2024 and reaffirmed the return to managed travel partnerships and TMC collaboration first announced in mid-2024. This reversal indicates:

*   **Management Acknowledgment:** Management explicitly reversed the strategy in mid-2024, responding to competitive market data and measurable yield pressure (reaffirmed on the Jan 23, 2025 earnings call).
*   **Operational Flexibility:** American adjusted strategy when competitive results indicated market share loss, demonstrating management's willingness to adjust strategy (earnings call Jan 23, 2025).
*   **Competitive Challenge Ahead:** Rebuilding corporate and travel-management-company (TMC) partnerships typically takes time; American cited "ongoing revenue management headwinds" in early 2025 (earnings release Jan 23, 2025) as those partnerships were being rebuilt.

American's Q1 2025 guidance reflected ongoing yield pressure from corporate travel partnership rebuilding. Q1 2026 actuals (reported April 23, 2026) confirmed the rebuilding is materializing: revenue of $13.91 billion was the highest first-quarter revenue in company history (+10.8% YoY), with managed corporate revenue up 13% year-over-year (Q1 2026 earnings release). In the June quarter total revenue rose 16.3% year over year on 5.4% more capacity, a company record. The rebuild is therefore no longer a forecast to be tested; it is showing in the fare line. What it has not done is reach earnings. American cut full-year 2026 adjusted earnings guidance twice in 2026 — to ($0.40) to $1.10 per diluted share in April, down from the $1.70 to $2.70 guided in January, and again in the July release to ($0.65) to $0.65, "given the recent increase in the cost of fuel." For the following quarter the company guides to available seat miles up 3.0% to 5.0%, total revenue up 16.0% to 19.0%, unit cost excluding net special items, fuel and profit sharing up 2.5% to 4.5%, an average fuel price of approximately $3.75 per gallon, and adjusted earnings of ($0.70) to ($0.10) per diluted share.

## Cost Structure and Operational Efficiency

### CASM Analysis and Cost Position

American's **CASM of 17.61¢** is 5.5% higher than United's 16.70¢/mile (2024 10-K filings). This cost disadvantage reflects several structural factors:

**Fleet Complexity:** American operates a diverse fleet including Boeing 737 (737-800 + 737 MAX 8), Boeing 787 widebodies, the Airbus A320 family (A319, A320, A321), and Embraer regional aircraft. The Boeing 767 fleet was [retired in 2020](https://news.aa.com/news/news-details/2020/American-Airlines-Accelerates-Retirement-of-Boeing-757s-and-767s-Plus-Other-Aircraft-CORP-FI-04/default.aspx) and Boeing 757s were accelerated for retirement at the same time. Even with that simplification, the remaining mix increases maintenance and crew-training costs relative to single-family fleets.

**Labor Costs:** American's pilot contract, ratified in 2023, included pilot-specific wage increases of approximately 40% ($9B total contract value, AA 10-K 2024). That is consistent with comparable large pilot-contract resets at Delta and United. Subsequent mainline flight attendant and passenger service team member agreements were ratified in 2024. These costs remain elevated.

**Airport Costs:** American's concentration at DFW and CLT reflects the cost structures at both airports. DFW is a capital-intensive large hub, reflecting its infrastructure investments and operating model. Both support the service quality and capacity that benefit American's network hub.

### Fleet Modernization Challenges

American has orders for Boeing 737 MAX aircraft to replace older 737-800 narrowbodies and for the Airbus A321XLR for long-haul narrowbody markets. Like all carriers, AAL faces Boeing + Airbus delivery delays. Following the [2020 retirement of 757s and 767s](https://news.aa.com/news/news-details/2020/American-Airlines-Accelerates-Retirement-of-Boeing-757s-and-767s-Plus-Other-Aircraft-CORP-FI-04/default.aspx), fleet modernization centers on continuing 737 MAX deliveries, 787 widebody utilization, A321XLR introduction, and regional carrier optimization. Fleet simplification and modernization remain priorities but are capital-intensive.

However, the airline shows ability to cover debt service obligations (10-K 2024): (1) American generated operating cash flow of $4.0B and free cash flow of $2.2B in FY2024, both records at the time — but FY2025 operating cash flow was $3.099 billion against $3.779 billion of capital expenditures and aircraft purchase deposits, and the FY2025 10-K prints no free cash flow figure at all, so the $2.2B is a FY2024 result rather than a run rate; (2) the negative equity reflects cumulative historical debt load and balance sheet accounting, not current operational distress; and (3) under conservative assumptions — at $2.2B FCF annually (2024 actual, net of capital expenditures), less $1.0B mandatory debt principal amortization and assuming zero dividend payments (per 10-K) — the airline could retain approximately $1.2B/year for discretionary debt reduction or liquidity rebuilding (book-equity recovery would depend on sustained retained earnings and favorable balance-sheet movements, not debt repayment by itself). This illustrative bridge isolates mandatory amortization and excludes larger refinanceable bullet maturities (current maturities of long-term debt and finance leases were $3.094 billion at June 30, 2026) and working-capital variability, and would require sustained operational consistency and stable revenue trends.

### Debt Reduction Achievement and Trajectory

American achieved its $15 billion total debt reduction goal from peak levels (mid-2021) in the fourth quarter of 2024 — a full year ahead of the original year-end 2025 timeline (AAL FY2024 results release). This reflects management's stated commitment to debt reduction (10-K 2024). As an illustrative DWU sensitivity — holding free cash flow at 2024's $2.2B and assuming roughly $1.0B of mandatory (non-bullet) amortization — on the order of $1.2B/year could be directed to discretionary debt reduction. This is a simplified bridge, not a figure drawn from the 10-K maturity schedule, which shows materially larger gross maturities (roughly $3.6B in 2026, $4.5B in 2027, and $7.3B in 2028) that are refinanced rather than repaid from free cash flow; it also excludes working-capital variability, and assumes constant FCF and revenue stability. DWU states no agency leverage estimate and no numeric upgrade sensitivity here, because neither is available through a channel it can cite: American's own FY2025 Form 10-K names no rating agency anywhere, agency research-update bodies are subscriber-gated, and Fitch Ratings' site is not reachable — so an "expected mid-4x" or "sub-4x" threshold attributed to an agency would be an unsourced number wearing an agency's name. What the filings support is the direction and not a level: leverage materially below current levels would be needed for an investment-grade profile, and rating agencies apply forward-looking ratio criteria rather than a fixed dollar or ratio trigger. The low $20 billions debt-reduction range is DWU illustrative scenario math, not a published agency dollar threshold; rating agencies apply ratio-based, forward-looking criteria rather than fixed debt levels.

**Required Path to Investment Grade:**

*   **Debt Reduction to the low $20 billions (DWU illustrative scenario):** Bringing lease-adjusted debt/EBITDAR down from the 7.9x DWU derives for FY2025 — reaching sub-4x would take roughly halving adjusted debt or doubling EBITDAR from the FY2025 level, and DWU states no agency's upgrade sensitivity because none is readable to it
*   **Leverage and Coverage Normalization:** Bringing lease-adjusted Debt/EBITDAR toward ~3.5x with improving FFO/Debt and liquidity — the ratio-based metrics on which investment grade is assessed (rebuilding book equity is a byproduct, not the rating test)
*   **Sustained Profitability:** Demonstrating sustained net income and cash generation over several years
*   **Operational Stability:** Resolving corporate travel yield headwinds and returning to consistent pricing power

## Available Liquidity and Debt Service Capacity

American held **$11.28 billion of total available liquidity at June 30, 2026** — cash of $1.028 billion, short-term investments of $6.742 billion and $3.510 billion of undrawn facilities — against $9.233 billion at December 31, 2025. **Not all of it is spendable.** A significant portion of American's debt agreements require it to maintain at least $2.0 billion of unrestricted cash and amounts available under revolving credit facilities in aggregate. So the headline figure overstates usable liquidity by that covenant floor, and the company says so in its own filing.

Measured against net interest expense of $1.716 billion in FY2025 the remaining cushion is real but not deep. The lower-leverage peers carried materially lower debt at year-end 2024 (investment-grade Delta with total debt and finance leases of about $16.2B, and near-investment-grade United at about $28.7B). That indicates American's thinner cushion relative to its debt size — though exact cross-carrier liquidity ratios mix periods and liquidity definitions.

With **FY2024 operating cash flow of $4B and free cash flow of $2.2B**, American had capacity to service its debt and continue modest debt reduction; in FY2025, operating cash flow of $3.099 billion fell short of $3.779 billion of capital expenditures and aircraft purchase deposits. However, net interest expense of roughly $1.9B annually is a heavy fixed charge; because free cash flow is already net of cash interest, the constraint shows up as limited post-interest free cash flow available for deleveraging once scheduled principal amortization is layered on. This debt service burden is higher than Delta's and United's, reflecting lease-adjusted debt/EBITDAR of 7.9x at American for FY2025, DWU's own arithmetic, against lower ratios at Delta and United. No Form 10-K prints the ratio for any of the three.

## Credit Rating and Outlook — High Yield Status

American's corporate credit is **non-investment grade**, and that is the company's own characterization rather than an outside assessment: its Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025 lists "our non-investment grade corporate credit rating" among the factors that may make raising capital difficult (Item 1A, Risk Factors; SEC accession 0000006201-26-000014). That sentence is the whole of what American discloses on the subject. The filing names no rating agency anywhere — its only two references to S&P are to the S&P 500 stock index in the Item 5 performance graph — and neither the second-quarter 2026 Form 10-Q nor the July 2026 earnings release mentions an agency either. **DWU therefore states the category only, and states no agency rating, outlook, action date, instrument rating or agency leverage estimate for any agency — not because none exists, but because DWU has no citable source for them.** Agency research-update bodies are subscriber-gated and Fitch Ratings' site is not reachable, and a rating claim sourced to a page the writer cannot open is not a rating claim. The rating is not merely a label at this company: American's revolving credit facilities carry an interest margin that steps with AAG's public corporate credit rating, so a downgrade reprices borrowing automatically, and a substantial part of the debt stack requires a floor of $2.0 billion of unrestricted cash and undrawn revolving capacity that the company therefore cannot spend. Key rating drivers include:

**Negative Factors:**

*   Negative total equity of ($4B)
*   Debt and finance leases of $28.927 billion at June 30, 2026 ($3.094 billion of current maturities and $25.833 billion long-term) against a $3.972 billion stockholders' deficit. Lease-adjusted debt/EBITDAR was 7.9x in FY2025 and 6.5x in FY2024. American's filings print no such ratio — the FY2025 Form 10-K does not contain the word EBITDAR. So this is DWU's own arithmetic on lines the filing does print: EBITDAR of $4.577 billion for FY2025 (operating income $1,467M plus depreciation and amortization $1,890M plus aircraft rent $1,220M) against adjusted debt of $35.97 billion (debt and finance leases $29,007M plus operating lease liabilities $6,963M). The range carried elsewhere on this page until September 2026 was two to four turns below this and DWU cannot attribute it to an agency
*   2024 corporate travel strategy reversal (AA earnings)
*   PRASM pressure and yield headwinds in 2024-2025
*   Limited financial flexibility for unexpected challenges
*   Competitive pressure from Delta and United, which carry materially lower lease-adjusted debt/EBITDAR than the 7.9x DWU derives for American in FY2025 — Delta reports 2.6x on its own adjusted basis, and DWU derives no figure for United here

**Positive Factors:**

*   FY2024 free cash flow of $2.2B, a post-merger record — though FY2025 operating cash flow of $3.099 billion did not cover $3.779 billion of capital expenditures and aircraft purchase deposits, and the FY2025 10-K prints no free cash flow figure
*   Successful ahead-of-schedule $15B debt reduction achievement
*   DFW and CLT hub dominance enabling pricing power and network efficiency (BTS T-100 2024)
*   AAdvantage cash payments from co-branded credit card and other partners of $6.2 billion in 2025 against $6.1 billion in 2024 — roughly 2% growth, not the 17% of 2024, which American says included a one-time payment tied to its new co-brand agreement
*   Management willingness to acknowledge and reverse strategic errors
*   Large passenger base and broad route network supporting resilience (BTS T-100 2024)

**Path to Investment Grade:** The recent corporate travel strategy reversal suggests some execution risk in the near-term, but the airline's fundamental network value remains intact.

## Competitive Analysis and Market Position

### vs. Delta Air Lines

Delta states in its own Form 10-K that it "is rated investment grade by each of the three major credit rating agencies," and that filing gives exactly one letter grade: Moody's upgraded Delta to Baa2 in February 2025. It also records that Fitch moved its outlook to Positive from Stable in the September 2025 quarter and that S&P Global did the same in January 2026, without stating either agency's grade. Against that, American's own filing states only that its corporate credit is non-investment grade. Delta also leads on profitability (net income $3.46B vs. American's $846M in FY2024, a 75% gap per 10-Ks) and operating margins (approximately 9.7% for Delta vs. lower for American). American's DFW hub operates at 84% market share concentration vs. Delta's Atlanta hub at 75% (BTS T-100 2024), providing American with marginally higher local market influence. Both airlines operate comparable loyalty programs (AAdvantage at American, SkyMiles at Delta); AAL discloses $6.1B in 2024 cash remuneration from AAdvantage marketing partnerships, while program-valuation estimates from third parties are not directly comparable across carriers. Overall, Delta's stronger profitability and lower leverage provide financial flexibility that American currently lacks.

### vs. United Airlines

United maintains higher equity ($12.7B vs. American's negative $4B per 10-Ks 2024) and lower lease-adjusted debt/EBITDAR than the 7.9x DWU derives for American in FY2025. United publishes its agency grid in its own Form 10-K: as of that filing United Airlines Holdings is rated BB+ by S&P Global, Ba1 by Moody's and BB+ by Fitch, with the outlooks given in the accompanying text as stable at Moody's and Fitch and positive at S&P. That is exactly why United's ratings can be stated here with outlooks and American's cannot: the disclosure differs, not the method. DWU states no agency action dates for either carrier, because the actions themselves are not readable through a channel it can cite. American's AAdvantage program ($6.1B in 2024 cash remuneration) matches United's MileagePlus in scale. Hub comparison: American's DFW concentration (84% market share, 925 of 1,100 departures) exceeds United's ORD concentration (42% of ORD departures (BTS T-100 2024, 487/1,150 daily flights), per BTS T-100 2024 analysis), giving American stronger hub pricing power. The competitive positioning is closer to Delta than during pre-merger American, but United's lower leverage and its materially higher agency ratings remain competitive advantages in capacity competition and debt refinancing.

### Domestic Network Dominance

American's DFW hub market share (84% of 1,100 daily departures, BTS T-100 2024) exceeds Delta's ATL concentration (75%, BTS T-100 2024) and United's ORD concentration (estimated 40-45% per T-100 analysis). This concentration provides American with significant pricing power and network efficiency. However, this concentration also creates vulnerability. If DFW market demand declines, if competing carriers aggressively expand ORD, or if business travel shifts away from Texas markets, American's yield recovery could be constrained. American's recovery strategy depends on sustained corporate travel in DFW and CLT markets.

## Strategic Priorities and Outlook

### Corporate Travel Partnership Rebuilding

Management's current priorities include TMC partnership rebuilding (Q4 2024 earnings call, Jan 23, 2025). Success is likely to depend on offering competitive corporate fares and incentives, maintaining reliable service and on-time performance, and delivering strong customer service. Management's explicit reversal of the prior strategy demonstrates this is a material priority for yield recovery. Historical precedent: Delta's post-2020 managed-travel recovery offers a broad benchmark (Delta earnings transcripts 2021-2022).

### Continued Debt Reduction

Management's stated 2026 target is to bring total debt below $35B (American Airlines Q1 2026 earnings release), and Q1 2026 total debt of $34.7B already met that threshold. The July 2026 release restates the commitment — the company "remains committed to reducing debt, lowering interest expense and achieving its leverage objectives" — without a dollar figure, and neither that release nor the Form 10-Q prints a company-defined total debt number at June 30, 2026. What they do print is the balance sheet: $3.094 billion of current maturities and $25.833 billion of long-term debt and finance leases, $28.927 billion on that narrower basis. Beyond the 2026 target, an illustrative path to investment-grade leverage (taken here as sub-4x adjusted debt/EBITDAR, a DWU assumption, since DWU cites no agency upgrade sensitivity) would require further reduction toward roughly the low-to-mid $20 billions — that lower band is DWU scenario math, not management guidance. The illustrative DWU sensitivity used earlier on this page (2024 free cash flow of $2.2B less roughly $1.0B of mandatory non-bullet amortization, with zero dividend payments) is FY2024 arithmetic that FY2025 did not repeat: operating cash flow of $3.099 billion fell short of $3.779 billion of capital expenditures and aircraft purchase deposits, so on FY2025 figures there was nothing left to direct at discretionary debt reduction — before the larger refinanceable bullet maturities and working-capital variability noted above. The timeframe depends on maintaining operational consistency and revenue stability.

### Fleet Modernization

Accelerating 737 MAX deliveries to replace older aircraft would improve unit costs and competitiveness. Boeing delivery delays are a constraint, but fleet modernization is necessary to improve unit costs and competitiveness.

### AAdvantage Program Monetization

AAdvantage cash payments from co-branded credit card and other partners reached $6.2 billion in 2025 from $6.1 billion in 2024 (FY2025 10-K). The program is also collateral, and increasingly so. American incurred $1.0 billion of incremental AAdvantage term loans in May 2025 and amended the facility again in February 2026. So the program is being financed against as well as monetized. American has indicated plans to continue developing this partnership through enhanced cardholder benefits and expanded distribution.

## Key Risks and Challenges

### Macroeconomic Recession Risk

American is heavily exposed to corporate travel and premium-cabin demand. In past downturns such as the 2008–2009 recession, fares and yields fell sharply for U.S. carriers, pressuring operating margins. A similar downturn would compress American's yields and require cost actions to protect profitability.

### Competitive Pressure and Market Share Losses

Delta and United maintain lower lease-adjusted debt/EBITDAR than American's 7.9x for FY2025 on DWU's arithmetic. That gives them greater financial flexibility to compete for corporate market share and key domestic markets. Aggressive capacity (available seat mile, ASM) growth has historically pressured unit revenue (PRASM) across the industry. If competitors expand capacity aggressively, American's yield recovery timeline could be compressed further.

### Boeing Delivery Delays Continued Impact

American's fleet modernization depends on timely 737 MAX deliveries, which remain uncertain. Extended delays would perpetuate cost disadvantages.

### Interest Rate and Refinancing Risk

American has significant debt maturing across 2026-2028, with the largest scheduled maturity bucket in 2028 (per 10-K debt schedule). That requires refinancing during a period of yield pressure. If market conditions deteriorate or credit spreads widen, refinancing costs could increase materially, as occurred for high-yield issuers during the 2008–2009 recession. American's refinancing capacity depends on demonstrating operational consistency and revenue stability during TMC partnership recovery.

### Labor Cost Inflation

AAL's FY2024 results included special-item charges from newly ratified mainline flight attendant and passenger service team member agreements (AA newsroom, FY2024 release). The pilot contract was previously settled in 2023 at approximately 40% wage increases ($9B total contract value, 10-K 2024). Recent airline labor contracts have included wage increases well above general consumer-price inflation. Future contract resets could pressure margins if revenue growth slows.

## Conclusion

American set a revenue record again in FY2025 at $54.633 billion and earned $111 million on it. That compares with $846 million on $54.211 billion in FY2024. Operating income fell $1.147 billion while revenue rose. The June 2026 quarter repeated the pattern at larger scale: a record $16.735 billion of revenue, up 16.3%, and $71 million of net income.

The airline still carries a stockholders' deficit of $3.972 billion at June 30, 2026 and $28.927 billion of debt and finance leases on its balance sheet. The execution question has shifted from corporate-travel yield to fuel. Management's explicit reversal of the 2023-2024 corporate travel strategy shows responsiveness to market feedback (earnings call Jan 23, 2025). The path to investment-grade credit ratings would likely involve sustained debt reduction (toward the low $20 billions), sustained positive net income over several years, and operational consistency in TMC partnership recovery.

From an equity perspective American remains the most leveraged way to own U.S. domestic airline recovery: a stockholders' deficit of $3.972 billion at June 30, 2026, more upside than Delta or United if the fare gains hold, and materially less cushion if they do not. From a credit perspective American describes its own corporate credit as non-investment grade (FY2025 Form 10-K, Item 1A); DWU states no agency rating, outlook or date, because it has no citable source for them. Lease-adjusted debt/EBITDAR is 7.9x for FY2025 on DWU's own arithmetic, up from 6.5x in FY2024 as operating income fell 43.9%. American's filings print no such ratio and DWU attributes it to no agency: it is the sum of debt, finance leases and operating lease liabilities divided by operating income plus depreciation and amortization plus aircraft rent, every input taken from AAG's FY2025 Form 10-K. Read it as DWU's measurement on the carrier's own printed lines, not as any agency's. The critical milestones have moved. The June 2026 quarter answered the revenue question at +16.3% year over year, a company record, so the open question is no longer whether the corporate-travel rebuild works but whether it can outrun fuel: a 77.1% rise in price per gallon turned a record top line into $71 million of net income and a second guidance cut, to full-year adjusted earnings of ($0.65) to $0.65 per diluted share. Refinancing of the 2026-2028 maturities, the largest bucket falling in 2028, still sets the cost-of-capital trajectory, and the $2.0 billion covenant floor inside the $11.28 billion liquidity figure is the constraint to read first.

## Introduction

American Airlines Group is the third-largest U.S. airline by 2025 operating revenue, behind Delta and United, and operates one of the most extensive U.S. route networks (DOT BTS data), connecting high-yield corporate markets through hubs in Dallas-Fort Worth (approximately 925 of about 1,100 daily departures, roughly 84%, based on 2024 DFW operating data and BTS T-100), Charlotte, and Miami. With **$54.2 billion in then-record full-year 2024 operating revenue** (since surpassed by FY2025's $54.6 billion), American demonstrated profitability with approximately 3% year-over-year revenue growth per the 2024 10-K; about 224 million passengers boarded its flights in 2025 (FY2025 Form 10-K). However, American's financial story reflects **$30.48 billion in long-term debt at year-end 2024 (the company's largest reported debt line; AAL's company-defined total debt — which includes finance and operating lease obligations and pension obligations — was approximately $39B at year-end 2024, the highest among the Big 3 carriers)** — and **negative total equity of approximately ($4 billion)**, putting lease-adjusted debt/EBITDAR at 7.9x for FY2025 — $35.97 billion of debt, finance leases and operating lease liabilities against EBITDAR of $4.58 billion, which is DWU's own arithmetic on four lines AAG prints in its FY2025 Form 10-K, against lower ratios at Delta and United. No Form 10-K prints this ratio for any of the three carriers; the arithmetic is shown in the leverage section below.

American's financial position reflects advantages (84% DFW hub share) and structural risks (lease-adjusted debt/EBITDAR of 7.9x for FY2025 on DWU's arithmetic, against lower peer ratios): (1) the airline operates its largest hub by daily departures (DFW with approximately 925 daily departures, about 84% of ~1,100 total, BTS T-100 2024; among the most single-carrier-concentrated large hubs, though American's Charlotte hub carries an even higher share), which enables connections to 300+ destinations and influences local fares (BTS T-100 2024); (2) the AAdvantage loyalty program produces approximately **$6.1 billion in annual cash remuneration** from co-branded credit-card and loyalty-marketing agreements (up 17% in 2024 per the 10-K) — a cash-flow measure recognized within passenger and other revenue, not a separate additive revenue line; this stream tends to be less volatile than passenger revenue; yet (3) a 2023-2024 strategy shift to direct corporate accounts weighed on American's unit-revenue (Passenger Revenue per Available Seat Mile, PRASM) performance relative to peers during 2024, prompting the reversal announced in mid-2024 (AA earnings calls); by the fourth quarter of 2024 American's passenger unit revenue had returned to year-over-year growth (AA Q4/FY2024 release). This profile examines American's financial structure, operational challenges, strategic recovery, and credit dynamics.

## Company Overview

### History and Structural Legacy

American Airlines was founded in 1926. That predates Delta (1928) and United (1926 reorganization) among major U.S. carriers. The 2013 merger with US Airways created American Airlines Group (AAG). It became the world's largest airline by fleet size (approximately 1,000 mainline aircraft plus regional partners, 10-K 2024) and passengers carried, surpassing Delta and United. The merger unified two legacy carriers with overlapping networks. It also created post-merger integration challenges documented in American's 2014-2016 10-K filings around fleet utilization, crew bases, and integration costs. See [Airline Bankruptcy and Restructuring History](https://dwuconsulting.com/dwu-ai/airline-bankruptcy-restructuring-history) for context on post-merger integration outcomes.

Headquartered in Fort Worth, Texas, American operates under International Air Transport Association (IATA) code **AA** and International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) code **AAL**. The airline maintains significant operations at [Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport (DFW)](https://web.archive.org/web/https://www.dfwairport.com/about/), its largest hub, and at [Charlotte Douglas International (CLT)](https://www.cltairport.com/), its second-largest hub. American is a founding member of the **Oneworld Alliance**, providing global codeshare access to British Airways, Japan Airlines, Cathay Pacific, and others.

As of 2024, American employs approximately 133,300 team members system-wide across all functions (10-K 2024). It is a major employer in the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex, where it is headquartered.

### Strategic Market Position

American operates a domestic network spanning corporate markets including New York, Washington DC, Los Angeles, Miami, Boston, and Philadelphia. The airline reported a 2024 PRASM of 16.93¢/mile (10-K 2024). About 224 million passengers boarded American's flights in 2025 (FY2025 Form 10-K).

#### Airport Planning Considerations

American's debt structure and negative equity matter for airport tenant-risk monitoring, traffic-risk scenario planning, and air-service strategy at the airports it dominates. They do not directly drive Passenger Facility Charge (PFC) spending, however. PFC use is governed by statutory eligibility, FAA approval, project funding structure, and the no-double-charge rules, not by a carrier's balance sheet. Airports may consider carrier credit metrics and debt refinancing schedules in scenario planning for revenue patterns and service continuity (DOT BTS data).

Conversely, American's 84% departure share at DFW (BTS T-100, 2024) provides the carrier with network leverage and pricing power. From the airport's perspective, however, single-carrier concentration above 50% is a credit-rating consideration under S&P and Fitch airport methodologies. DFW's investment-grade rating rests on underlying revenue resilience, liquidity, its rate-setting methodology and AUA protections, strategic importance, and a substantial non-airline revenue base, even as American's departure share remains high. PFCs can offset eligible capital and debt service but are restricted, project-specific revenues. Debt-service-coverage covenants are bondholder protections and tests rather than diversification mechanisms in their own right. Free cash flow: $2.2B (2024 10-K).

## Hub Network and Competitive Positioning

### Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW) — American's Largest Hub by Daily Departures

Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) is American's flagship hub with approximately 84% of daily departures (about 925 of 1,100 daily departures based on DFW airport operating data + BTS T-100 2024; mainline departures inclusive of regional affiliates). American controls approximately 925 daily departures and serves more than 230 nonstop destinations from DFW. This roughly 84% departure share exceeds Delta's approximately 75% at Atlanta and United's share at Chicago ORD (BTS T-100 2024), providing American with:

**Network Leverage:** Domestic connectivity via 300+ destinations (BTS T-100 2024). A passenger from Austin, San Antonio, or anywhere in the Texas, Oklahoma, or Arkansas region can reach virtually any major U.S. market through DFW, often with a single connection.

**Pricing Power:** At DFW's 84% departure share, American's hub concentration supports network pricing power and can influence local fares in some markets (Dallas to New York, Dallas to Los Angeles). Route-level fare effects, however, depend on origin-and-destination (O&D) demand and competitive capacity rather than departure share alone.

**Operational Efficiency:** The scale of DFW operations — 925 daily American flights out of DFW's 1,100 total daily flights — justifies investment in premium ground infrastructure, crew scheduling, and customer service.

**Corporate Travel Concentration:** DFW serves the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex, a metro area of approximately 8.3 million people (U.S. Census Bureau). It is home to corporate headquarters including Texas Instruments (technology), AT&T (telecommunications), and American Airlines Group (aviation), along with numerous Fortune 500 companies. This corporate base generates premium-cabin and business-travel demand from major employers.

### Charlotte (CLT) — Second Hub and Growth Market

Charlotte Douglas International Airport is American's second-largest hub, where American holds a high share of daily departures and serves a broad domestic network (BTS T-100 2024). CLT anchors American's hub in Charlotte's banking and corporate market (the Research Triangle/Raleigh-Durham region is served by its own airport, RDU). The Charlotte metropolitan area has been among the faster-growing large U.S. metros (U.S. Census Bureau). American's hub status at CLT provides strong pricing influence.

### Miami (MIA) — Caribbean and Latin American Gateway

Miami serves as American's Latin American and Caribbean gateway, serving as a gateway to major Caribbean and Latin American markets (BTS T-100 2024). Miami-Dade County has a majority-Hispanic population (U.S. Census Bureau), supporting connectivity to Central and South America (BTS T-100 2024).

## Strategic Shifts and 2024 Adjustments

### Corporate Travel Strategy Shift

In 2023-2024, American management under CEO Robert Isom shifted to direct corporate accounts. That weighed on the airline's unit-revenue (PRASM) performance relative to peers during 2024 (AA 2024 earnings calls). The shift created several challenges.

**The challenges of the strategy:** Corporate travelers book through their companies' preferred travel management companies (TMCs like American Express Global Business Travel, BCD Travel, etc.), which receive commissions from airlines and can negotiate volume discounts. American's attempt to bypass TMCs and shift corporate bookings to direct channels led to reduced bookings via TMCs (AA Q4 2024 earnings).

**Competitive Disadvantage:** Delta and United maintained strong TMC partnerships and actively competed for corporate business, capturing market share from American. Corporate travel yields higher fares, more first/business class upgrades, and better liquidity profile — making this loss particularly damaging.

**Yield Compression:** American's PRASM lagged competitors particularly in mid-2024 (AA 2024 earnings calls).

### Management Acknowledgment and Strategic Reversal

On the Q4 2024 earnings call (January 23, 2025), CEO Robert Isom acknowledged that American's 2023-2024 corporate travel strategy had weighed on the airline's unit-revenue performance during 2024 and reaffirmed the return to managed travel partnerships and TMC collaboration first announced in mid-2024. This reversal indicates:

*   **Management Acknowledgment:** Management explicitly reversed the strategy in mid-2024, responding to competitive market data and measurable yield pressure (reaffirmed on the Jan 23, 2025 earnings call).
*   **Operational Flexibility:** American adjusted strategy when competitive results indicated market share loss, demonstrating management's willingness to adjust strategy (earnings call Jan 23, 2025).
*   **Competitive Challenge Ahead:** Rebuilding corporate and travel-management-company (TMC) partnerships typically takes time; American cited "ongoing revenue management headwinds" in early 2025 (earnings release Jan 23, 2025) as those partnerships were being rebuilt.

American's Q1 2025 guidance reflected ongoing yield pressure from corporate travel partnership rebuilding. Q1 2026 actuals (reported April 23, 2026) confirmed the rebuilding is materializing: revenue of $13.91 billion was the highest first-quarter revenue in company history (+10.8% YoY), with managed corporate revenue up 13% year-over-year (Q1 2026 earnings release). In the June quarter total revenue rose 16.3% year over year on 5.4% more capacity, a company record. The rebuild is therefore no longer a forecast to be tested; it is showing in the fare line. What it has not done is reach earnings. American cut full-year 2026 adjusted earnings guidance twice in 2026 — to ($0.40) to $1.10 per diluted share in April, down from the $1.70 to $2.70 guided in January, and again in the July release to ($0.65) to $0.65, "given the recent increase in the cost of fuel." For the following quarter the company guides to available seat miles up 3.0% to 5.0%, total revenue up 16.0% to 19.0%, unit cost excluding net special items, fuel and profit sharing up 2.5% to 4.5%, an average fuel price of approximately $3.75 per gallon, and adjusted earnings of ($0.70) to ($0.10) per diluted share.

## Cost Structure and Operational Efficiency

### CASM Analysis and Cost Position

American's **CASM of 17.61¢** is 5.5% higher than United's 16.70¢/mile (2024 10-K filings). This cost disadvantage reflects several structural factors:

**Fleet Complexity:** American operates a diverse fleet including Boeing 737 (737-800 + 737 MAX 8), Boeing 787 widebodies, the Airbus A320 family (A319, A320, A321), and Embraer regional aircraft. The Boeing 767 fleet was [retired in 2020](https://news.aa.com/news/news-details/2020/American-Airlines-Accelerates-Retirement-of-Boeing-757s-and-767s-Plus-Other-Aircraft-CORP-FI-04/default.aspx) and Boeing 757s were accelerated for retirement at the same time. Even with that simplification, the remaining mix increases maintenance and crew-training costs relative to single-family fleets.

**Labor Costs:** American's pilot contract, ratified in 2023, included pilot-specific wage increases of approximately 40% ($9B total contract value, AA 10-K 2024). That is consistent with comparable large pilot-contract resets at Delta and United. Subsequent mainline flight attendant and passenger service team member agreements were ratified in 2024. These costs remain elevated.

**Airport Costs:** American's concentration at DFW and CLT reflects the cost structures at both airports. DFW is a capital-intensive large hub, reflecting its infrastructure investments and operating model. Both support the service quality and capacity that benefit American's network hub.

### Fleet Modernization Challenges

American has orders for Boeing 737 MAX aircraft to replace older 737-800 narrowbodies and for the Airbus A321XLR for long-haul narrowbody markets. Like all carriers, AAL faces Boeing + Airbus delivery delays. Following the [2020 retirement of 757s and 767s](https://news.aa.com/news/news-details/2020/American-Airlines-Accelerates-Retirement-of-Boeing-757s-and-767s-Plus-Other-Aircraft-CORP-FI-04/default.aspx), fleet modernization centers on continuing 737 MAX deliveries, 787 widebody utilization, A321XLR introduction, and regional carrier optimization. Fleet simplification and modernization remain priorities but are capital-intensive.
